newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwanda opens genocide trial of alleged ringleader. [CORRECTED 15:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Rwanda opens genocide trial of alleged ringleader. [CORRECTED 15:40 GMT]

text.p: Rwanda put on trial on Tuesday a prominent politician accused of being a ringleader of the 1994 genocide of minority Tutsis masterminded by Hutu extremists -- despite being an ethnic Tutsi himself.

Froduald Karamira was a vice-president of the extremist MDR-Power party under the ousted Hutu-led government and is the most senior suspect held in Rwanda on charges of taking part in the mass slaughter of some 800,000 people.

Karamira was born a Tutsi but using a Rwandan custom he converted to become a member of the Hutu tribe, the majority that ruled Rwanda until Tutsi rebels ousted them from power and put an end to the three months of killings in July 1994.

Karamira is accused of being a leader of the Interahamwe militia that led the attacks in the capital Kigali and was allegedly responsible for inciting genocide through broadcasts on state-run Radio Rwanda and Radio Mille Collines (RTLM).
His defence lawyer, Paul Atita (corrects name) from Benin, immediately applied for an adjournment of 15 days saying he had never met his client before and had not prepared himself for the case.
"I want a postponement as well," Karamira told the court.

Presiding judge, Jariel Rutaremara, told the court he accepted the request and adjourned the trial until January 29. The trial, by a panel of three judges, of four little-known Hutus charged along with Karamira would continue later on Tuesday, the judge said.
The five men face death by firing squad if convicted.
The international human rights group, Amnesty International, has expressed concern at the conduct of Rwanda's genocide trials. Some suspects have had no defence lawyers.
Defence witnesses laughed as they were called to the dock to identify themselves in Kigali on Tuesday.
"Why do you think I am here?" laughed Odette Mushashi, as she presented herself before the judges. "I am here to testify him," she said pointing at Karamira.
Rwanda's prosecutor has assembled 23 witnesses to testify against Karamira, who was arrested at Ethiopia's Addis Ababa airport last June and extradited to Rwanda.

"I see Froduald Karamira as one of the men directly responsible for the massacres in Rwanda," an African missionary who fled the parish of Kabgayi after the massacres told the human rights group African Rights.

"Immediately after the plane crash (in which Hutu President Juvenal Habyarimana was killed), every single day, Karamira gave an interview to the RTLM radio making the most inflammatory statements," the missionary said.
Rwanda holds about 90,000 people suspected of taking part in the genocide but has only just started putting them on trial. Two Hutu men were sentenced to death in Kibungo on January 3.

Trials also opened on Tuesday in the town of Nyamata of two Hutu men accused of genocide. Officials named them as Alexis Dusingize, a former government official of Kanzenze commune in Nyamata, and a former customs driver identified as Mvunabandi.
Prosecution officials said Dusingize presided over Kanzenze commune, which included the church at Nyamata, where an estimated 6,000 Tutsis were slaughtered.
Hutu militias from Kanzenze commune were also responsible for the killings at Ntarama church in Nyamata parish, where more than 5,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus were killed.
The United Nations is holding a separate series of trials of Rwandan genocide suspects in Arusha, northern Tanzania.

On Tuesday Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former mayor of central Taba commune, continued to cross-examine the first prosecution witness, known only by the letter "K" to protect her identity. Presiding Judge Laity Kama granted the accused's request to cross-examine personally the first witness to appear before the U.N. tribunal.
